## Review: What Is a Dashboard Scientifically?

- A dashboard is a coordinated analytical environment in which each visual component is deliberately selected, positioned, and linked to support a predefined decision workflow

- Unlike static figures in a paper, dashboards encode process:

  - which evidence is allowed to influence the decision
  - what questions are expected to be asked
  - the order the scientific questions are addressed

::: footer

:::

## Identifying the Dashboard Primary User

- dashboard support specific decision-makers
- collaborators (i.e.: clinicians, translational scientists, biostatisticians) will interpret evidence differently and prioritize different signals
- a single dashboard can have different visual priorities depending on the audience 
- dashboards are designed to reflect the interests of the audience

::: footer
:::

## <span style="font-size:80%">Biomedical Code Example: Simulated Trial Monitoring Dashboard</span> {.smaller}

- Dashboards for clinical trial patient monitoring integrate multiple evidence streams: enrollment, safety, efficacy, and protocol compliance
- Data presented in the dashboard could inform high-stakes actions such as pausing enrollment or escalating safety reviews

::: footer

:::


## <span style="font-size:80%">Biomedical Code Example: Simulated Trial Monitoring Dashboard</span> {.smaller}

- In the following code example, we’ll explore the following clinical or translational trial data:

  - Enrollment data : responsibility to ensure recruitment is on track and representative
  - Safety data : responsibility to detect adverse events and protect participant welfare
  - Efficacy data : responsibility to assess whether the intervention is showing benefit
  - Protocol compliance data : responsibility to ensure the trial is being conducted correctly and consistently

::: footer

:::

## <span style="font-size:80%">Biomedical Code Example: Simulated Trial Monitoring Dashboard</span> {.smaller}

- Example shows how the use of a dashboard for monitoring clinical trial results organizes multiple types of information that are reviewed in parallel during an ongoing study
- illustrates how multiple streams of data can be displayed together without implying that one outcome is more important than another
- consistent layout, shared time axes, and clearly defined denominators allows users to compare trends across panels while keeping each metric tied to its specific monitoring purpose
- structure of the dashboard makes it easier to interpret changes in one stream—such as enrollment or adverse events

::: footer

:::


## <span style="font-size:80%">Summary</span> {.smaller}

- Designing interactive dashboards for research use involves creating analytical environments that keep multiple forms of evidence visible, aligned, and interpretable
- Clinical monitoring dashboard shows how multiple research-relevant evidence streams—enrollment, safety, efficacy, and protocol compliance—can be organized within a single interface so they are interpreted together, rather than as isolated outcomes
- dashboard design for research use can account for changing exposure and sample size
- Designing interactive dashboards for research use, the use of a consistent layout and shared time axes demonstrates how design choices can support meaningful comparison across panels while preserving the distinct analytical role of each metric
